name: PCM3060PWR
title: PCM3060: 24-bit, 96/192 kHz asynchronous stereo audio codec
summary: A stereo audio codec in a 28-pin TSSOP: a 24-bit delta-sigma ADC with single-ended inputs (16 to 96 kHz) and a 24-bit delta-sigma DAC with differential or single-ended outputs (16 to 192 kHz). The ADC and DAC each take their own system clock and audio port, so they can run at unrelated sample rates, each as master or slave, in I2S, left-justified or right-justified format. Attenuation, soft mute, de-emphasis, filter roll-off and power save are set through an SPI or I2C port, or three basic functions are set by pins in hardware mode. Analog runs from 5 V and digital from 3.3 V.

circuits.title: Typical connection
circuits.description: The codec between a control microcontroller, an audio receiver or encoder feeding the ADC port, and an audio transmitter or decoder fed by the DAC port. The microcontroller drives the three shared control pins and RST. Both analog inputs come in through 4.7 µF electrolytic capacitors, positive side at the chip, sized for a 3 Hz cutoff. The four DAC outputs, both zero flags and VCOM go to an external low-pass filter and buffer; VCOM also biases the input source. VCC, VDD and VCOM each carry a 10 µF electrolytic beside a 0.1 µF ceramic. All four grounds join. MODE goes to one of four terminations that pick the control mode.

circuits.description: An inverting op-amp stage scales a 2 Vrms line signal to the ADC's input range: gain 0.5 (R2/R1) with a 48 kHz corner. The non-inverting input sits at VCOM, decoupled by C3. C1 blocks the source's DC. R3 and two diodes, one to a supply rail and one to ground, clamp the voltage reaching VINx. The op amp runs from split rails, each bypassed by an electrolytic.

where.fS: sampling rate: 16 to 96 kHz for the ADC, 16 to 192 kHz for the DAC

operation.text: SCKI1 clocks the ADC and SCKI2 the DAC, so the two halves can run from unrelated clocks. For synchronous use one clock on either pin can drive both, chosen with CSEL1 (register 72) or CSEL2 (register 67) in software mode.

ADC system clock: 256, 384, 512 or 768 fS with fS from 16 to 96 kHz. DAC system clock: 128, 192, 256, 384, 512 or 768 fS with fS from 16 to 192 kHz. The 128 fS and 192 fS ratios and the 176.4 and 192 kHz rates are DAC only. Minimum clock period is 25 ns, duty cycle 40% to 60%.

An internal power-on reset acts once VDD passes about 2.2 V. In hardware mode with RST high, internal reset ends 1024 SCKIx cycles after power-up. In software mode with RST high, it ends 1024 SCKIx cycles after ADPSV and DAPSV are cleared over the control port. Holding RST low keeps the part in reset until RST rises. The DAC outputs follow VCOM (0.5 VCC) as VCC comes up. With SCKIx, BCKx and LRCKx in step, the DAC begins fading in 2048/fS after reset ends (tDACDLY1) and reaches the DIN signal 1616/fS later (tDACDLY2); DOUT likewise starts fading in after 2048/fS (tADCDLY1) and carries the input signal 1936/fS after that (tADCDLY2). Without clock synchronisation the part stays in reset and power-down; once the clocks lock, both halves run their fade-in.

RST held low for at least 2048/fS (tRST) forces a reset and puts the device in power-down, its lowest-power state. With clocks running, the DAC outputs fade out over 1616/fS to VCOM and DOUT fades to zero over 1936/fS; then the device resets and powers down, clearing every register and memory except the mode control registers. Raising RST runs the power-on sequence again. The clocks may stop during power-down but must be running again before power-up. Setting ADPSV and DAPSV gives the same fade-out and fade-in on DOUT and the DAC outputs.

The ADC and DAC ports are each set to slave or master independently; slave is the default for both. DIN is always an input and DOUT always an output. As slave, BCK and LRCK are inputs and BCK must be 64 fS or 48 fS. As master, the device derives BCK and LRCK from its system clock and BCK is 64 fS. In both, BCK2 rising edges sample DIN and BCK1 falling edges update DOUT.
Each port takes 24-bit I2S, 24-bit left-justified, 24-bit right-justified or 16-bit right-justified, in master or slave mode, chosen separately for ADC and DAC. All are MSB first, two's complement.

No particular phase between the audio clocks and SCKI is needed, but their frequencies must stay locked. If SCKI2 and LRCK2 drift apart by more than ±6 BCK2 periods (BCK2 = 64 fS) or ±5 (BCK2 = 48 fS), the DAC stops within 2/fS and its outputs hold at VCOM until the clocks relock and tDACDLY3 (22/fS) passes. The same drift between SCKI1 and LRCK1 stops the ADC within 2/fS and holds DOUT at zero until relock plus tADCDLY3 (32/fS). Drift under ±5 periods (64 fS) or ±4 (48 fS) causes no resynchronisation. Undefined data during the loss, and the jumps into and out of it, can be heard as noise. If the system clock stops, DOUT and the DAC outputs hold their last state.
VINL and VINR are single-ended inputs, each taking 0.6 VCC peak-to-peak with about 10 kΩ input resistance.

VOUTL and VOUTR are differential pairs biased at VCOM, each giving 0.8 VCC peak-to-peak per pin (1.6 VCC peak-to-peak differential) into a 10 kΩ DC-coupled load. An on-chip continuous-time RC filter trims the modulator's out-of-band noise, though for many uses an external low-pass filter is still needed. The MODE pin or the S/E bit switches to single-ended, where VOUTx+ is the output and VOUTx– is left open.

VCOM is an unbuffered 0.5 VCC output, the internal common and reference voltage for both converters, brought out for decoupling. It can bias outside circuitry if that load is high against its 12.5 kΩ typical output resistance.

The ADC oversamples at 64 fS. The DAC runs at 64, 32 or 16 fS, picked from the ratio of system clock to sampling rate, and the OVER bit doubles it to 128, 64 or 32 fS. Doubling can lower out-of-band noise but may slightly change in-band performance, and writing OVER while running may pop.

Each DAC channel flags zero data after 1024 consecutive zero samples on DIN. ZEROL and ZEROR can drive an external mute or report to a controller. AZRO picks per-channel flags or both flags for both channels at zero; ZREV inverts them from active high to active low.

MODE is sampled at power-on or external reset and later changes are ignored until the next reset. Tied to DGND it selects I2C; 220 kΩ to DGND, hardware mode with differential outputs; 220 kΩ to VDD, hardware mode with single-ended outputs; tied to VDD, SPI. The resistor is 220 kΩ ±5%. In hardware mode three pins set the interface (IFMD), format (FMT) and de-emphasis (DEMP), each applied to both converters.

MS (select, active low), MC (clock) and MD (data) form a port that runs independent of the audio clocks. A write is a 16-bit word: a 0, the 7-bit register index IDX[6:0], then 8 data bits D[7:0], MSB first. MS goes low, 16 MC clocks shift the word in, and MS going high latches it. Holding MS low and clocking further bytes after the first word writes successive registers; MS high ends the burst.

The device is an I2C slave receiver for standard and fast mode (fast mode with up to 100 pF bus load). Its 7-bit address is 100011 followed by the level of ADR (pin 27), so two devices can share a bus. A write sends the address with the write bit, a register address, then data; in a multi-byte write the register index steps up by one per byte and wraps from 4Ah back to 40h. Undefined registers are not acknowledged. Register addresses and data are 8 bits, MSB first.

Writing MRST = 0 returns the mode registers to their defaults; SRST = 0 resynchronises the clocks and restarts both converters without clearing registers or powering down. Both bits return to 1 by themselves, and both may cause a pop.

ADPSV and DAPSV default to 1, power save, so in software mode both must be cleared before the converters run. Entering power save fades DOUT to zero or the DAC outputs to VCOM, resets that converter's data and powers it down; leaving it fades back in. Each change needs more than 2048/fS. The control port stays live. Clock changes, clock stops and interface-mode changes are best made while powered down, to avoid pops and degraded performance.

operation.topic: Digital attenuation and soft mute, DAC
operation.text: Each DAC channel has an attenuator from 0 to –100 dB in 0.5 dB steps plus mute. The level moves one 0.5 dB step every 8/fS toward the target. A new command during a ramp waits in a one-deep buffer, the latest overwriting the earlier, and runs when the ramp ends. MUT2x = 1 ramps the channel to mute at the same rate; clearing it ramps back to the set level.

operation.topic: Digital attenuation and soft mute, ADC
operation.text: Each ADC channel has a gain stage from +20 dB to –100 dB in half-decibel steps plus mute. With zero-cross detection on (ZCDD = 0) each step lands on a zero crossing of the input, checked every 1/fS; if none comes within 512/fS, steps go every 1/fS until a crossing appears. With ZCDD = 1 a step goes every 8/fS. Commands buffer as in the DAC. MUT1x ramps to mute and back the same way.

FLT picks sharp (default) or slow roll-off for the DAC interpolation filter. DMC turns on de-emphasis and DMF picks 44.1, 48 or 32 kHz for it. DREV2 inverts the DAC output phase and DREV1 the ADC input phase. BYP bypasses the ADC high-pass filter; bypassed, the DC of the input and the internal DC offset are converted too.

VDD and VCC each take a 0.1 µF ceramic plus a 10 µF electrolytic to their own ground, mounted right at the pins. Running VCC from a 5 V supply and deriving VDD's 3.3 V from that same 5 V avoids latch-up and similar trouble from wrong power sequencing.
AGND1, AGND2, SGND and DGND are separate inside the device. Join them with low impedance directly under the part.

A 4.7 µF electrolytic coupling capacitor gives a 3 Hz corner. A larger full-scale input is had with one series resistor at VINx, at the cost of some gain error from the spread of the input resistance: with 9.1 kΩ in series the full scale becomes 2 Vrms and the gain error is near 10%.
VCOM takes a 0.1 µF ceramic plus a 10 µF electrolytic to AGND, mounted right at the pin, to keep the reference source impedance low.

A differential-input buffer and filter stage can be wired to the outputs directly, without coupling capacitors, for a 2 Vrms output. In single-ended mode VOUTL+ and VOUTR+ are the outputs and VOUTL– and VOUTR– stay open.

Converter performance depends on SCKI1/2 jitter, duty cycle and edge times. Although the two system clocks may be unrelated, one common clock is preferred unless two base rates such as 44.1 and 48 kHz are needed.

As slave no particular phase between BCK/LRCK and SCKI is needed, though some phase relationships can degrade performance and controlling that phase can cure it. As master, heavy loads on BCK, LRCK and DOUT can degrade performance; keep them light.

To power down and up without the pop from the DAC output's DC step, the order is: engage the external mute; put the codec in power-down; halt and restart SCKI1/SCKI2 if needed; take the codec out of power-down; release the external mute.
